Characterizations of E-finite algebras

When do the cones of two-term silting complexes cover every integral projective class? For a finite-dimensional algebra, the answer can be read from morphisms between its modules, from the distribution of its bricks, or from its wide subcategories.

Theorem A. Over any field, an algebra is E-finite precisely when every two nonzero finite modules of the same composition vector admit a nonzero homomorphism in each direction. This is also equivalent to finiteness of every semibrick and to the absence of generic bricks.
Theorem B. An algebra with at most two simple right modules up to isomorphism is E-finite if and only if it has finitely many bricks up to isomorphism, equivalently if and only if it is τ-tilting finite.

Verification and provenance

What changes with the field?

A brick has a division ring of endomorphisms. Counting bricks by their dimension over this division ring characterizes E-finiteness over every field. Over an infinite field one may instead count them by their ordinary composition vectors. Over an algebraically closed field there are also geometric tests using open orbits, open wide loci and closed points of King moduli spaces.

The manuscript and the library

The statement correspondence locates each of the 44 numbered results in Lean, including the finite-field and localization arguments in the appendices. The declaration index links the main results to their definitions and proofs.
